Corollary III.3.

Two pairs of qudit Werner states with parameters ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB} and ΨA​C−\Psi^{-}_{AC} are joinable if and only if ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−≥−12\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC}\geq-\frac{1}{2}, or if the parameters satisfy

(ΨA​B−+ΨA​C−)2+13​(ΨA​B−−ΨA​C−)2≤1,(\Psi^{-}_{AB}+\Psi^{-}_{AC})^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(\Psi^{-}_{AB}-\Psi^{-}_{AC})^{2}\leq 1, (46)

or additionally, in the case d≥3d\geq 3, if ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−≤12\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC}\leq\frac{1}{2}.

Proof.

To obtain these conditions, it suffices to project the shape given in Eq. (36) onto the ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB}-ΨA​C−\Psi^{-}_{AC} plane. The rim of the cone/bicone projects down to an ellipse whose equation we obtain by extremizing Eq. (35) evaluated at the cone base Ψ−¯=0\overline{\Psi^{-}}=0. Setting ΨB​C−=−ΨA​B−−ΨA​C−\Psi^{-}_{BC}=-\Psi^{-}_{AB}-\Psi^{-}_{AC}, we find the boundary to be 1=(ΨA​B−+ΨA​C−)2+13​(ΨA​B−−ΨA​C−)21=(\Psi^{-}_{AB}+\Psi^{-}_{AC})^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(\Psi^{-}_{AB}-\Psi^{-}_{AC})^{2}. Any pairs of Werner states within this ellipse are joinable. We also have that ΨA​B−=1\Psi^{-}_{AB}=1 and ΨA​C−=1\Psi^{-}_{AC}=1 are joinable since setting ΨB​C−=1\Psi^{-}_{BC}=1 causes the three to satisfy Eq. (35). Then, by the convexity of the set of joining states, the convex hull of (ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−)=(1,1)(\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC})=(1,1) and the ellipse corresponds to pairs of joinable states. If d≥3d\geq 3, the states ΨA​B−=−1\Psi^{-}_{AB}=-1 and ΨA​C−=−1\Psi^{-}_{AC}=-1 are joinable by setting ΨB​C−=−1\Psi^{-}_{BC}=-1, and hence the joinable (ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−CLOSE(\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC}) pairs also include the convex hull of the ellipse with the point (ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−)=(−1,−1)(\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC})=(-1,-1).

It remains to show that if ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB} or ΨA​C−≤−12\Psi^{-}_{AC}\leq-\frac{1}{2} (additionally, ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB} or ΨA​C−≥12\Psi^{-}_{AC}\geq\frac{1}{2} for d≥3d\geq 3), then (ΨA​B−,ΨA​C−)(\Psi^{-}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{AC}) pairs outside of the ellipse are not joinable. To achieve this, we consider a cone viewed from an arbitrary direction an infinite distance away. The shape seen is the shape of the projection. From this vantage point, the circular base of the cone appears as an ellipse. The remaining visible area (seen only if the vertex does not overlap with the base) constitutes the projection of the cone’s lateral surface. The boundary of this projection is defined by the two lines extending from the vertex that are tangent to the ellipse. The area contained between these two lines along with the hull of the ellipse constitutes the shape visible from the infinity perspective, or, in other words, the cone’s projection. In our case, the points at which these two lines (four lines for the bicone) intersect the ellipse are (−1/2,1)(-1/2,1) and (1,−1/2)(1,-1/2) (additionally, (−1,1/2)(-1,1/2) and (1/2,−1)(1/2,-1) for the bicone). Beyond these points, the ellipse “takes over” as the projection boundary delimiter. Thus, points satisfying ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB} or ΨA​C−≤−12\Psi^{-}_{AC}\leq-\frac{1}{2} (and, ΨA​B−\Psi^{-}_{AB} or ΨA​C−≥12\Psi^{-}_{AC}\geq\frac{1}{2} for the bicone) are joinable if and only if they are within the ellipse boundary. ∎

Corollary III.4.

Two pairs of qudit isotropic states with parameters ΦA​B+\Phi^{+}_{AB} and ΦA​C+\Phi^{+}_{AC} are joinable if and only if they lie within the convex hull of the ellipse

(ΦA​B+/d+ΦA​C+/d−1)2(1/d2)+(ΦA​B+/d−ΦA​C+/d)2(d2−1)/d2=1,\frac{(\Phi^{+}_{AB}/d+\Phi^{+}_{AC}/d-1)^{2}}{(1/d^{2})}+\frac{(\Phi^{+}_{AB}/d-\Phi^{+}_{AC}/d)^{2}}{(d^{2}-1)/d^{2}}=1, (47)

and the point (ΦA​B+,ΦA​C+)=(0,0)(\Phi^{+}_{AB},\Phi^{+}_{AC})=(0,0).

Proof.

We follow the approach of the proof of Corollary III.3 above, by projecting the cone described by Eqs. (43)-(44) down to the ΦA​B+\Phi^{+}_{AB}-ΦA​C+\Phi^{+}_{AC} plane. The rim of the cone projects down to an ellipse whose equation we obtain by extremizing Eq. (43) evaluated at the cone base ΦA​B++ΦA​C+−ΨB​C−=d\Phi^{+}_{AB}+\Phi^{+}_{AC}-\Psi^{-}_{BC}=d. Setting ΨB​C−=ΦA​B++ΦA​C+−d\Psi^{-}_{BC}=\Phi^{+}_{AB}+\Phi^{+}_{AC}-d, we find the boundary to be 1=|(ΦA​B++ΦA​C+−d)+i⁡(ΦA​B+−ΦA​C+)/d2−1|1=\left|(\Phi^{+}_{AB}+\Phi^{+}_{AC}-d)+i(\Phi^{+}_{AB}-\Phi^{+}_{AC})/\sqrt{d^{2}-1}\right|. From this we easily obtain the ellipse described by Eq. (47). Any pairs of Werner states within this ellipse are joinable. We also have that ΦA​B+=0\Phi^{+}_{AB}=0 and ΦA​C+=0\Phi^{+}_{AC}=0 are joinable since setting ΨB​C−=1\Psi^{-}_{BC}=1 causes the three to satisfy Eq. (43). The convex hull of the ellipse and the point (0,0)(0,0) exhausts the set of joinable pairs of isotropic states. ∎

Lastly, we explicitly provide the Werner-isotropic hybrid 1-2 joining boundary:

Corollary III.5.

An isotropic state with parameter ΦA​B+\Phi^{+}_{AB} and a Werner state with parameter ΨB​C−\Psi^{-}_{BC} are joinable if and only if they lie within the convex hull of the ellipse

(ΦA​B+/d+ΦA​C+/d−1)2(1/d2)+(ΦA​B+/d−ΦA​C+/d)2(d2−1)/d2=1,\frac{(\Phi^{+}_{AB}/d+\Phi^{+}_{AC}/d-1)^{2}}{(1/d^{2})}+\frac{(\Phi^{+}_{AB}/d-\Phi^{+}_{AC}/d)^{2}}{(d^{2}-1)/d^{2}}=1, (48)

and the point (ΦA​B+,ΨB​C−)=(0,1)(\Phi^{+}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{BC})=(0,1), and, for d≥3d\geq 3, within the additional convex hull introduced by the point (ΦA​B+,ΨB​C−)=(0,1)(\Phi^{+}_{AB},\Psi^{-}_{BC})=(0,1).

Proof.

Obtained in an analogous manner to Corollaries III.3 and III.4. ∎

Appendix B Proof of Werner state 11-nn sharability and construction of mm-nn sharability

Here, we set up the necessary background, then determine the 1-nn sharability of Werner states, while providing a constructive approach to determing mm-nn sharability. For fixed mm, nn, we only need to determine the most-entangled Werner state (largest value of −Ψ−-\Psi^{-}) satisfying that sharability property; as noted in Sec. II.2, all mixtures of that state with any separable state will necessarily satisfy the sharability property. Thus, in the one-dimensional convex set parameterized by Ψ−\Psi^{-}, the most-entangled Werner state that satisfies a sharability property indicates the boundary between the satisfying and the failing region.

The next step is to map the problem of determining the most-entangled Werner state for a given sharability criterion to the problem of determining the maximal eigenvalue of a particular operator. Specifically, we show that the most-entangled mm-nn sharable Werner state has concurrence equal to the largest eigenvalue of the operator

Hm,n=1m​n​∑i∈L∑j∈R(−Vi​j),H_{m,n}=\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{i\in L}\sum_{j\in R}(-V_{ij}),

and that a valid mm-nn sharing state wm,nw_{m,n} is given by the normalized projector into the corresponding eigenspace.

We first justify the construction of Hm,nH_{m,n}. From Eq. (5), the concurrence of a Werner bipartite reduced state of a composite system state ρ\rho is 𝒞i​j=−Tr​(Vi​j⊗𝕀i​j¯​ρ)\mathcal{C}_{ij}=-\text{Tr}\left(V_{ij}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{\overline{ij}}\rho\right). So, for a state ρm,n\rho_{m,n}, with each LL-RR pair a Werner state, its expectation with respect to Hm,nH_{m,n} is simply the average concurrence of its LL-RR pair reduced states.

Now, that the normalized projector into an eigenspace of Hm,nH_{m,n} is a valid sharing state follows from the symmetries of this operator: collective unitary invariance ensures that the reduced states are Werner states, while left-system permutation invariance and right-system permutation invariance ensure the mm-nn sharing property. That the maximal eigenvalue of Hm,nH_{m,n} is the concurrence of the most-entangled mm-nn sharable Werner state follows from the fact that if any state wm,n′w_{m,n}^{\prime} were to share Werner states with larger concurrence, its (the sharing state’s) expectation value with respect to Hm,nH_{m,n} would exceed the maximum eigenvalue, which is a contradiction.

It follows that, by determining the largest eigenvalue of Hm,nH_{m,n} for each value of mm and nn, we will have characterized the sharability properties of all Werner states. To determine the eigenvalues of Hm,nH_{m,n}, we express the latter in terms of quadratic Casimir operators on NN-fold tensor product of the (defining) dd-dimensional representations of 𝔰​𝔲​(d)\mathfrak{su}(d), namely, operators of the form

ΛN2\displaystyle\Lambda_{N}^{2} ≡Λ→N⋅Λ→N=∑α=1d2−1(ΛNα)2,\displaystyle\equiv\vec{\Lambda}_{N}\cdot\vec{\Lambda}_{N}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d^{2}-1}\left(\Lambda_{N}^{\alpha}\right)^{2},

where ΛNα=∑i=1N(𝕀1⊗…⊗λiα⊗…⊗𝕀N)\Lambda_{N}^{\alpha}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbb{I}_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes\lambda^{\alpha}_{i}\otimes\ldots\otimes\mathbb{I}_{N}) and {λiα}\{\lambda^{\alpha}_{i}\} span each of the NN local 𝔰​𝔲​(d)\mathfrak{su}(d) Lie algebras. By construction, any such Casimir operator commutes with all the elements of the (generally reducible) tensor-product algebra. By rewriting each swap operator as Vi​j=𝕀/d+∑αλiα​λjαV_{ij}=\mathbb{I}/d+\sum_{\alpha}\lambda^{\alpha}_{i}\lambda^{\alpha}_{j}, we obtain

Hm,n=\displaystyle H_{m,n}= −𝕀d−1m​n​∑i∈L∑j∈R∑αλiα​λjα\displaystyle-\frac{\mathbb{I}}{d}-\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{i\in L}\sum_{j\in R}\sum_{\alpha}\lambda^{\alpha}_{i}\lambda^{\alpha}_{j} (49)
=\displaystyle= −𝕀d−12​m​n{∑α[∑k∈L∪Rλkα]2−∑α[∑i∈Lλiα]2\displaystyle-\frac{\mathbb{I}}{d}-\frac{1}{2mn}\bigg\{\sum_{\alpha}\Big[\sum_{k\in L\cup R}\lambda_{k}^{\alpha}\Big]^{2}-\sum_{\alpha}\Big[\sum_{i\in L}\lambda_{i}^{\alpha}\Big]^{2}
−\displaystyle- ∑α[∑j∈Rλjα]2}=12​m​n(ΛL2+ΛR2−ΛL​R2)−𝕀d.\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\Big[\sum_{j\in R}\lambda_{j}^{\alpha}\Big]^{2}\bigg\}=\frac{1}{2mn}\left(\Lambda_{L}^{2}+\Lambda_{R}^{2}-\Lambda_{LR}^{2}\right)-\frac{\mathbb{I}}{d}.

Two relevant features of tensor-product Casimir operators are worth noting. First, ΛN2\Lambda_{N}^{2} will not simply be proportional to the identity operator, but rather, on each irreducible subspace it will act as a (possibly) different multiple of identity. Secondly, the operator ΛN2⊗𝕀M\Lambda^{2}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{M} commutes with ΛN+M2\Lambda^{2}_{N+M} for any MM and NN.

The three Casimir operators ΛL​R2\Lambda_{LR}^{2}, ΛL2\Lambda_{L}^{2}, and ΛR2\Lambda_{R}^{2} mutually commute and it is thus meaningful to seek their simultaneous eigenvalues. Each eigenvalue of a tensor product Casimir operator corresponds to an irreducible subspace WiW_{i} and hence to a Young diagram. The latter may be used to compute the value of the corresponding eigenvalue. Following [60], given a Young diagram YY of column heights {ai}\{a_{i}\} and row lengths {bj}\{b_{j}\}, the eigenvalue of the corresponding space of the Casimir operator is

CY=N⁡(d−Nd)+∑jbj2−∑iai2.C_{Y}=N\left(d-\frac{N}{d}\right)+\sum_{j}b_{j}^{2}-\sum_{i}a_{i}^{2}. (50)

The eigenspaces of ΛL​R2\Lambda_{LR}^{2} which intersect with a given ΛL2\Lambda_{L}^{2} eigenspace and a given ΛR2\Lambda_{R}^{2} eigenspace may be calculated by pasting together the boxes of a YLY_{L} and a YRY_{R} Young diagram in a way that does not cause two previously symmetrized boxes (same row) to then be antisymmetrized (same column), and vice versa. Writing AY=∑iai2A_{Y}=\sum_{i}a_{i}^{2} and BY=∑jbj2B_{Y}=\sum_{j}b_{j}^{2}, and replacing each Casimir operator in Eq. (49) with its its eigenvalue given by Eq. (50), we find that the sum of the first terms of the eigenvalues cancels with 𝕀/d\mathbb{I}/d, leaving

eig​(Hm,n)=AYL​R−AYL−AYR−BYL​R+BYL+BYR2​m​n.\text{eig}(H_{m,n})=\frac{A_{Y_{LR}}-A_{Y_{L}}-A_{Y_{R}}-B_{Y_{LR}}+B_{Y_{L}}+B_{Y_{R}}}{2mn}. (51)

Thus, we have a prescription for calculating the eigenvalues of Hm,nH_{m,n}. In particular, we obtain the maximal eigenvalue of Hm,nH_{m,n} by constructing the optimal set of three Young diagrams, as exploited in the following:

Theorem III.6.

A qudit Werner state with parameter Ψ−\Psi^{-} is 11-nn sharable if and only if

Ψ−≥−d−1n.\Psi^{-}\geq-\frac{d-1}{n}. (52)
Proof.

All that is necessary is to use Eq. (51) to obtain the largest eigenvalue of H1,nH_{1,n}. The maximal eigenvalue of H1,nH_{1,n} is realized by the following gluing of the 11 and nn-box Young diagrams

  

⊗\otimes      …\dots          ⋮\vdots                                                                                                                    ⇒\Rightarrow         …\dots          ⋮\vdots       .                                                                                                            

The values of the AA and BB here are AYL​R=d2+n+1−dA_{Y_{LR}}=d^{2}+n+1-d, AYL=1A_{Y_{L}}=1, AYR=(d−1)2+n+1−dA_{Y_{R}}=(d-1)^{2}+n+1-d, and BYL​R=BYL+BYR=(n+2−d)2+d−1B_{Y_{LR}}=B_{Y_{L}}+B_{Y_{R}}=(n+2-d)^{2}+d-1, which allow us to compute the maximal eigenvalue of H1,nH_{1,n},

max​(H1,n)=d−1n.\text{max}(H_{1,n})=\frac{d-1}{n}. (53)

Therefore, the desired conclusion follows. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
